name: The Pioneer Woman Chili
writer_notes: All 16 locked ingredients are used by a step; no step uses an unbought item.

Source labels diced tomatoes as 'Instant Pot version only', but the build BUYS 34 oz diced tomatoes for the batch, so I folded them into the single stovetop-pot method (bought means must be used). Flag for QA if the intent was to drop them.
Source also lists Tortilla Chips/Fritos and cornbread; these are NOT in the locked buy list, so they appear in no step and are listed in forbidden_prose_terms.
Cost written as ${{cost_ps}} token because no cost_ps figure was supplied in the locked view; macros written as {{cal}}/{{protein}} tokens. No numbers computed by me.
Scaling from source to 14-serving buy is internally consistent at ~2.33x across every line (beef, beans, tomato sauce, spices, masa, garlic, diced tomatoes); no quantity flags.
Collapsed the source's three parallel methods (stovetop, crock pot, Instant Pot) into one faithful stovetop-pot method to match a single container-based meal-prep card.

prose.intro_html:
Chili is the meal-prep workhorse nobody gives enough credit to. It is cheap, it freezes like a champion, and it gets better the second and third day while your fancier recipes are busy going sad in the fridge. This is the Pioneer Woman version, built on 80/20 ground beef, a double hit of beans, and a little masa harina to pull the whole pot together into something with real body instead of soup with ambition.

Here is the part I like. One batch fills fourteen containers, each one lands around {{cal}} calories with {{protein}} grams of protein, and the whole thing costs about ${{cost_ps}} per serving. That is a hot, filling, high-protein dinner for less than a drive-through side. You cook once, you eat all week, and you keep your money.
prose.shop_smart:
The beef is your biggest line, so buy the 80/20 when it is on sale and freeze what you do not use today. Leaner grinds cost more and give you less of the richness that makes chili taste like chili, so there is no bargain in trading up here.

Beans are where the budget wins. You need kidney and pinto, and the standard cans stack up to the amount you want without any fuss. Buy the store brand, drain and rinse them yourself, and skip the pre-seasoned cans that charge you extra for salt you already own.

The spice list looks long but it is your everyday pantry crew: chili powder, cumin, oregano, salt, and cayenne. If you cook at all, you already have most of it, and a jar of chili powder stretches across many batches. Masa harina is the one shelf item worth seeking out. It is cheap, it lives in the baking or international aisle, and one bag thickens pot after pot. Grab the tomato sauce and diced tomatoes in whatever can size adds up to the amounts on the list, and pick up the garnishes, cheddar, sour cream, limes, and green onions, only if you want them, because the chili stands on its own without a single one.
prose.make_it:
Get a large heavy pot over medium heat and cook the ground beef, crumbling it as it goes, until it is browned through. Drain off the excess grease, because that fat is calories you do not need and it is already counted in your numbers.

Add the diced garlic and the tomato sauce and cook it for a minute, just long enough to knock the raw edge off the garlic. Now add the seasonings all at once: the chili powder, cumin, oregano, salt, and cayenne. Stir until every bit of beef is coated, then drop the heat to low.

Cover the pot and let it simmer for about an hour, stirring now and then so nothing catches on the bottom. If it looks dry along the way, stir in a splash of water. While it simmers, whisk the masa harina with a little water in a small bowl until it is a smooth slurry with no lumps, then stir that into the chili. This is what gives the pot its thickness and that slightly toasty corn flavor, so add a little more masa or water until it looks the way you want it.

Add the drained and rinsed kidney and pinto beans along with the diced tomatoes and their juice. Stir gently, then let it simmer another ten minutes so the beans warm through and everything marries. Taste it, adjust if it needs it, and you are done. Serve it out with shredded cheddar, a spoon of sour cream, a squeeze of lime, and a scatter of green onions if you are dressing it up.
prose.portion_html:
Do not eyeball this one. Weigh the empty pot before you cook so you know its bare weight, then weigh the full pot when the chili is done and subtract. Take that total and divide by fourteen, and that number is how many grams go in each container. It is the only honest way to make every serving hit the same {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein instead of one lucky container getting all the beef.

Ladle it evenly across your fourteen containers, let them cool, then lid and stack. It keeps well in the fridge for the week and freezes beautifully if you want to push some past that. Reheat covered with a splash of water if it has thickened up, and it comes back to life like day one.
prose.cost_closing_html: Here is the math that matters. Fourteen full, hot, high-protein dinners out of one pot, at about ${{cost_ps}} a serving. Cook this on a Sunday and you have handled a week of dinners for the price most folks spend on one lunch out. That is the whole idea of eating this way: buy smart, cook once, and let the freezer do the rest.
prose.upsell_html: If this is the kind of cooking that makes sense to you, the whole Thrifty Crew library runs on the same simple promise: real food, honest macros, and a plan that respects your wallet. Membership is a dollar a month. One batch of this chili already paid for the year, so come get the rest of the recipes.

head.description: The Pioneer Woman Chili scaled for meal prep: 14 hearty containers of 80/20 ground beef, kidney and pinto beans, and masa-thickened tomato base at about 680 calories and 41.8 g protein each. Budget-friendly, freezer-ready, high-protein dinner.

steps: Cook and crumble the ground beef in a large heavy pot over medium heat until browned, then drain off the excess grease.
Add the diced garlic and tomato sauce and cook for one minute to soften the garlic.
Stir in the chili powder, cumin, oregano, salt, and cayenne until the beef is evenly coated, then reduce the heat to low.
Cover and simmer for about one hour, stirring occasionally and adding a splash of water if the pot looks dry.
Whisk the masa harina with a little water into a smooth lump-free slurry, then stir it into the chili to thicken, adding more masa or water to reach the consistency you want.
Add the drained and rinsed kidney and pinto beans along with the diced tomatoes and their juice, then simmer another ten minutes until warmed through.
Weigh the pot, divide the chili evenly across 14 containers, and serve with shredded cheddar, sour cream, lime wedges, and diced green onions if desired.
